concepts.name: Alexander's Route of Invasion and Key Battles in the Indian Subcontinent
key_dimensions: Entry via Khyber Pass (327 BCE) and sequence of territorial conquests — Taxila, Hydaspes, Hyphasis
Battle of Hydaspes (326 BCE) against Porus: outcome, Alexander's respect for Porus, reinstatement as vassal
Distinction between northwestern frontier kingdoms encountered vs. Magadha (which Alexander never reached)
Why Alexander halted at Beas (Hyphasis): mutiny of troops, Nanda army strength as deterrent — a frequent UPSC trap

concepts.name: Political Vacuum Created by Alexander's Withdrawal and Its Consequences
key_dimensions: Fragmentation of Greek satrapies in northwest India after Alexander's death (323 BCE)
How the power vacuum directly enabled Chandragupta Maurya's westward expansion
Difference between territories Alexander 'conquered' vs. territories he could 'hold' — a trap distinction
Role of Seleucus Nicator as successor and eventual defeat by Chandragupta (305 BCE)

concepts.name: Chandragupta Maurya's Rise: Alexander's Invasion as a Catalyst
key_dimensions: Tradition of Chandragupta meeting Alexander (Justin's account) — historicity and debate
Chandragupta's use of mercenaries and tactical lessons from Greek military organization
Kautilya-Chandragupta alliance timed with post-Alexandrian instability in the northwest
UPSC trap: Alexander's invasion did not directly overthrow Nandas — Chandragupta did later

concepts.name: Greek Accounts as Historical Sources for Ancient India
key_dimensions: Key Greek writers — Arrian (Anabasis), Diodorus Siculus, Curtius Rufus, Strabo, Plutarch — and what each records
Megasthenes' Indica as a post-Alexandrian source: limitations and value
Information on Indian polity, society, caste, cities, and military from Greek accounts — corroboration with indigenous sources
UPSC trap: Megasthenes visited Chandragupta's court, NOT Alexander's — chronological distinction critical

concepts.name: Synchronism Between Greek and Indian Chronology
key_dimensions: Alexander's invasion (327–325 BCE) as a fixed chronological anchor for Indian history
How Sandrokottos = Chandragupta Maurya identification by William Jones established Indian chronology
Importance of this synchronism for dating Nanda dynasty, Buddha, and Mahavira
UPSC trap: Without the Greek synchronism, ancient Indian chronology before Ashoka is largely uncertain

concepts.name: The Battle of Hydaspes (326 BCE): Military and Political Significance
key_dimensions: Porus's kingdom (Paurava) — location between Jhelum and Chenab rivers
Military tactics: Greek use of cavalry vs. Indian war elephants — lessons learned by both sides
Alexander's post-battle policy: reinstatement of Porus as a subordinate ally, not annexed territory
Contrast with treatment of Ambhi (Taxiles) who surrendered vs. Porus who fought — different treatment, same outcome

concepts.name: Ambhi of Taxila and the Policy of Collaboration
key_dimensions: Ambhi (Omphis) voluntarily submitted to Alexander — political pragmatism vs. resistance
Taxila as a pre-existing center of learning and commerce: its importance to Alexander's campaign
UPSC trap: Ambhi's collaboration is often used to contrast with Porus — both ended as vassals under different paths
Implications for northwestern Indian polity: fragmented kingdoms made unified resistance impossible

concepts.name: Alexander's Retreat: Reasons and Significance of the Hyphasis Mutiny
key_dimensions: Immediate cause: soldiers' refusal to cross Beas — psychological exhaustion after 8 years of campaign
Intelligence about Nanda army strength (Xandrames/Agrammes in Greek sources = Dhana Nanda) as a deterrent
Alexander's route of return: down the Indus, through Gedrosia desert — not a triumphant march
Significance: demonstrates limits of Macedonian power and indirectly elevated Magadha's prestige

concepts.name: Greek Satrapies in Northwest India: Administration and Legacy
key_dimensions: Satrapies established by Alexander: Taxila, Sindh, Punjab — governors appointed (Philip, Peithon)
Instability: multiple Greek governors assassinated by local populations, showing shallow control
Transition from Alexandrian satrapies to Seleucid control after 323 BCE
Long-term legacy: foundation for later Indo-Greek kingdoms (Bactrian Greeks) — a distinct later phase, not Alexander himself

concepts.name: Cultural and Intellectual Exchange: Hellenism and Indian Thought
key_dimensions: Alexander's encounters with Indian philosophers: 'Gymnosophists' (naked philosophers) — possibly Jain or Ajivika ascetics
Onesicritus's account of dialogue with Dandamis and Calanus — Greek fascination with Indian asceticism
Calanus accompanying Alexander to Persia and his self-immolation — symbolic cultural encounter
UPSC trap: Hellenistic influence on Gandhara art came AFTER Alexander via Indo-Greek kingdoms, not directly from Alexander's invasion

concepts.name: Gandhara Art and the Indo-Greek Cultural Legacy
key_dimensions: Gandhara school of art: Greek artistic techniques applied to Buddhist themes — anthropomorphic Buddha image
Distinction: Alexander's invasion created the contact zone, but Gandhara art flourished under Kushanas (1st–3rd CE)
UPSC trap: Alexander's invasion is a root cause but NOT the immediate trigger of Gandhara art — chronological gap of 300+ years
Mathura school comparison: indigenous tradition vs. Gandhara's Hellenistic influence — a classic exam comparison

concepts.name: Economic Impact: Opening of Trade Routes Between India and the West
key_dimensions: Alexander's campaign mapped the northwestern land routes — later used for Mauryan and Silk Road trade
Establishment of Alexandria-on-the-Indus and other Greek cities as trade nodes
Post-Alexandrian Greek commercial interest in India: precursor to later Indo-Roman trade
UPSC angle: Economic integration of northwest India with Hellenistic world as a long-term consequence

concepts.name: Nanda Dynasty's Role as an Indirect Beneficiary and Victim
key_dimensions: Fear of Nanda army (reportedly 200,000 infantry, 80,000 cavalry, 6,000 war elephants per Greek sources) stopped Alexander
Irony: Nanda power deterred Alexander but could not prevent Chandragupta — who used post-Alexandrian instability
Greek accounts (Agrammes/Xandrames) being the only contemporary foreign reference to the Nanda dynasty
UPSC trap: Alexander never fought the Nandas — their military reputation alone influenced his decision

concepts.name: Seleucus–Chandragupta Treaty (305 BCE): A Direct Consequence of Alexander's Invasion
key_dimensions: Seleucus Nicator attempted to reclaim Alexander's Indian territories — defeated by Chandragupta
Treaty terms: Chandragupta received territories east of the Indus (including parts of modern Afghanistan); gave 500 war elephants
Diplomatic marriage alliance between Mauryas and Seleucids — opening of formal Greek-Indian diplomacy
Megasthenes sent as ambassador to Pataliputra — the treaty's direct consequence enabling Greek accounts of Mauryan India

concepts.name: Alexander's Administrative Innovations and Their Influence on Mauryan Statecraft
key_dimensions: Greek concept of centralized provincial administration (satrapy system) possibly influencing Mauryan provincial governance
Debate among historians: Did Kautilya's Arthashastra borrow administrative ideas from Greek/Persian models?
Similarities between Greek polis governance and Indian nagara administration — coincidence or influence?
UPSC trap: Direct causal link between Alexander's administration and Mauryan system is debated — avoid overstating the connection

concepts.name: Military Technology Transfer: War Elephants, Cavalry Tactics, and Siege Warfare
key_dimensions: Greeks learned the strategic value of war elephants from India — Seleucids and later Hellenistic powers used them extensively
Indian exposure to Macedonian phalanx and siege warfare techniques (e.g., at Aornos/Pir-Sar)
Chandragupta's military: possibly integrated Greek mercenaries and tactical innovations
UPSC angle: Military exchange as a two-way process, not just Greek influence on India

concepts.name: Historiographical Debate: Extent of Alexander's 'Impact' on Indian History
key_dimensions: Nationalist historians (e.g., R.C. Majumdar) downplayed Alexander's impact — India resumed normalcy quickly
Western historians overstated the 'civilizing' role of Alexander — colonial historiographical bias
Romila Thapar's view: Alexander's invasion significant mainly for Greek-Indian contact, not for internal Indian political change
UPSC relevance: Questions may ask candidates to 'critically assess' — need balanced view, not a one-sided narrative

concepts.name: Republic Tribes (Sanghas/Ganas) of Northwest India and Their Resistance
key_dimensions: Malavas, Kshudrakas, Sibis, Agalassoi — republican oligarchies that fiercely resisted Alexander
Contrast with monarchical states like Taxila that submitted easily — republican martial tradition
Alexander's wounding at Multan (Malli town) during siege of a Malava settlement — evidence of fierce resistance
UPSC trap: These republics are often overshadowed by Taxila/Porus narrative — their resistance is a high-yield lesser-known fact

concepts.name: Coinage and Numismatic Evidence of Indo-Greek Contact
key_dimensions: Punch-marked coins in circulation during Alexander's period — contrast with Greek coinage introduced later
Indo-Greek kings (post-Alexander) issued bilingual coins (Greek + Kharosthi/Brahmi) — evidence of cultural synthesis
UPSC trap: Alexander himself did not introduce coins to India — pre-existing punch-marked coinage was already sophisticated
Numismatic evidence as a primary source for reconstructing Indo-Greek history where textual sources are absent

concepts.name: Kharosthi Script: Spread as a Legacy of Northwestern Contact
key_dimensions: Kharosthi script (written right to left) derived from Aramaic — the administrative script of the Achaemenid Empire that preceded Alexander
Alexander's conquest of Persia brought him into contact with Aramaic-using regions — indirect link to Kharosthi's spread in India
Used in Ashoka's northwestern edicts (Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra) — evidence of its currency in the region
UPSC trap: Kharosthi's origin is pre-Alexandrian (Achaemenid) but its continued use in northwest India post-Alexander is part of the same contact zone legacy
